title: 12 years. 4 exits. 12 battle cards.
subtitle: Screenshot-sized lessons from building startups, and why I'm bringing the format back.

content.text: When I started Battle Cards in 2020, the premise was simple. Startups are a game of speed, speed means more mistakes, and the only real defence against mistakes is learning from them faster than they pile up. The trouble is that reading more is not the same as getting better. You can finish a book a week and still make the same mistake every quarter, because the lesson never made it from the page into a habit.

So I started writing what I called screenshot-sized essays: one idea, small enough to fit on a phone screen, built to be saved and actually used. The structure is simple, and it now has exactly three parts. What the idea is. Why it holds up. How to use it this week.

Then life got busy, which is a polite way of saying a few companies happened. Scapic, the no-code AR and VR platform, was acquired by Flipkart. Cope.Studio was acquired by Polygon. Reality Tools was acquired by MotionPage. Dehidden was acquired by Layer-E. Each of those taught me things I wish I had written down at the time, and mostly didn't.

I'm bringing the format back now for a specific reason, which ties into what I'm building at ShopOS: an AI lab that rolls up creative studios, so that the internet isn't full of slop. One of the ideas I keep coming back to, and that I write about at length in
Brands Are RL Environments

, is that judgement is the scarce thing now. Generation is cheap. Anyone can produce a hundred posts, a hundred decks, a hundred "lessons from my startup journey" threads. What is scarce is the filter: the few things that survived contact with reality and are still true years later.

That is what these cards are meant to be. They are not a listicle of everything I believe. They are the twelve I keep returning to, the ones that have survived four exits and a fair number of things that did not exit at all. Screenshot the ones that hit, and ignore the rest.

This is the original Battle Card, more or less. The point is not to read less; it is to close the loop between reading and doing. One lesson a week, turned into one rule, used before you go looking for the next lesson.

Every founder falls in love with the idea first; I certainly did. But customers never meet your idea. They meet the execution: the onboarding, the support reply, the thing that breaks on a Tuesday. Love the problem, date the idea, and judge everything by whether people actually use it.

The next big thing usually looks like a toy at first, which is exactly why incumbents ignore it. People play with things long before they pay for them. When someone dismisses something as "just a toy," that is often the most useful signal you will get all month.

No single mentor can cover your whole life. A small personal board, three to five people who each root for you in one specific area, is far more useful. The trick is to ask them how they would think about a problem, not what you should do; you want better questions, not borrowed answers.
Role models are a trap because nobody is great at everything, and copying a whole person means copying their flaws too. Collect traits instead. One a week, practised in your own voice.

The real enemy in the lean stretches is inertia, and it grows inside your own four walls. Get out. Meet people who run their days differently, ask how they do it, and steal one habit to try for a month.

After Scapic's acquisition I wrote about a map of reflection that got me through a strange few months. Reflection is scary when it is vague; a map makes it concrete. Scope runs from project to team to company. People sit on one side and product on the other. The last six months go on top, the next six months below.

Once the map is drawn, mark it. Heart the work you loved. Star the work teammates say you are uniquely good at. Cross out the work that drains you, and find someone who loves it. Your energy is telling you what your job should be.

I drew a version of this as a 2x2 for a fund this year. Short, simple tasks are a tool problem, so buy the tool. Long, hard tasks, the ones with memory and a hundred stacked decisions, are a people problem. They need someone who keeps going.

This is the newest card, and the one most tied to what I'm building now. Generation is cheap; judgement is scarce. Always make more drafts than you need, kill most of them, and write down why. Every kill teaches the system something.
We named Scapic partly because the domain was available, and half the world spelled it wrong for years. It still got acquired. Names feel enormous on day one. Day one thousand matters far more.

Nobody warns you that the day after an exit can feel strangely empty. Write the playbook while it is fresh, map what you loved and what you hated, and then start the next thing on purpose rather than by accident.
That's the set. If one of these helped, forward it to one founder who needs it today.
